The answer turns on two axes: whether labeled outputs are\n36\tavailable, and whether the learner interacts with its environment sequentially\n37\tor processes a fixed dataset.\n38\t\n39\t#strong[Supervised learning] sits at one end of the label-availability spectrum:\n40\tevery training example comes paired with a target output, so the learner\n41\treceives explicit corrective feedback on each prediction. #strong[Unsupervised\n42\t  learning] occupies the opposite end, working with raw data and no labels at\n43\tall; its goal is to discover structure (clusters, latent factors, density\n44\testimates) rather than to match a known answer. #strong[Semi-supervised\n45\t  learning] falls between the two, combining a small labeled set with a much\n46\tlarger unlabeled corpus, a practical compromise when annotation is expensive but\n47\traw data is plentiful. #strong[Self-supervised learning] sidesteps human labels\n48\tentirely by manufacturing its own supervision from the data's internal\n49\tstructure: masking a word in a sentence and predicting it, or predicting the\n50\tnext video frame from previous ones.\n51\t\n52\tAlong the second axis, #strong[reinforcement learning] is fundamentally\n53\tinteractive and sequential. The agent takes an action, observes a reward signal\n54\tand a new state, then chooses again; feedback is sparse, delayed, and tied to\n55\tthe consequences of its own choices rather than handed to it in a tidy label\n56\tcolumn. #strong[Active learning] is also interactive but in a different way: the\n57\tlearner queries an oracle (often a human annotator) for the label of a\n58\tstrategically chosen example, aiming to reach high accuracy with as few queries\n59\tas possible.\n60\t\n61\t@fig:machinelearningparadigmsataxonomy lays out these paradigms along the two\n62\taxes, showing how label availability and the sequential/interactive nature of\n63\tdata access together organize the landscape of learning approaches. Interactive/Sequential\n117\t\n118\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:53 '* Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (1/3)'\n119\t// Slide: Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (1/3)\n120\t#strong[Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (1/3)]\n121\t\n122\tHow do you set up a machine learning problem? The answer depends on what kind of\n123\tdata you have and what kind of feedback the learning system receives. There are\n124\tfive major paradigms, each suited to a different setting.\n125\t\n126\t#strong[Supervised learning] trains a model on labeled data: each input comes\n127\tpaired with the correct output, and the model learns to predict that output for\n128\tnew, unseen inputs. Image classification is a canonical example, where\n129\tarchitectures like ResNet learn to map pixel arrays to category labels using the\n130\tmillions of labeled photographs in ImageNet.\n131\t\n132\t#strong[Unsupervised learning] works without any labels at all. Instead, the\n133\tgoal is to discover hidden patterns or structure lurking in the data itself.\n134\tK-means clustering for customer segmentation is a typical application: the\n135\talgorithm groups customers by purchasing behavior without anyone telling it what\n136\tthe groups should be.\n137\t\n138\t#strong[Reinforcement learning] takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather\n139\tthan learning from a fixed dataset, the agent learns through interaction with an\n140\tenvironment, taking actions and receiving rewards or punishments that shape its\n141\tfuture behavior. Deep Q-Learning, which learned to play Atari games at\n142\tsuperhuman levels #cite(\"mnih2015dqn\"), demonstrated how powerful this\n143\ttrial-and-error paradigm can be when combined with deep neural networks.\n144\t\n145\t#strong[Self-supervised learning] bridges the gap between supervised and\n146\tunsupervised approaches by generating pseudo-labels directly from unlabeled\n147\tdata. The model creates its own supervision signal, typically by hiding part of\n148\tthe input and predicting the missing piece. BERT's masked language modeling\n149\tobjective #cite(\"devlin2019bert\") is a prominent example: the model masks random\n150\twords in a sentence and learns to reconstruct them, building rich language\n151\trepresentations in the process without a single human-provided label.\n152\t\n153\t#strong[Semi-supervised learning] combines a small set of labeled examples with\n154\ta much larger pool of unlabeled data to improve performance beyond what either\n155\tsource alone could provide. Named entity recognition illustrates this well: a\n156\thandful of sentences annotated with entity tags (person, organization, location)\n157\tcan be paired with vast quantities of raw text documents, letting the model\n158\tleverage the structure of natural language to generalize far beyond the limited\n159\tannotations.\n160\t\n161\tEach paradigm makes different assumptions about the available supervision\n162\tsignal, and choosing the right one is often the first and most consequential\n163\tdecision in framing a machine learning problem.\n164\t\n165\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:74 '* Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (2/3)'\n166\t// Slide: Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (2/3)\n167\t#strong[Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (2/3)]\n168\t\n169\t#strong[Online learning] trains a model incrementally from a stream of data\n170\tarriving in real time, rather than requiring the entire dataset up front. A\n171\tpractical example is online logistic regression for click-through rate\n172\tprediction, where the model updates its weights after each user interaction\n173\trather than retraining on a stored batch.\n174\t\n175\t#strong[Multi-task learning] trains a single model to perform multiple related\n176\ttasks simultaneously, exploiting shared structure across those tasks. For\n177\tinstance, a model might learn both sentiment analysis and question answering at\n178\tthe same time, allowing representations useful for one task to benefit the\n179\tother.\n180\t\n181\t#strong[Meta-learning], often described as #emph[learning to learn], equips a\n182\tmodel to adapt quickly to new tasks by leveraging prior experience across many\n183\tearlier tasks. A model trained this way can be fine-tuned on a new task using\n184\tjust a few gradient steps #cite(\"finn2017maml\"), dramatically reducing the data\n185\tand compute needed for each new problem.\n186\t\n187\t#strong[Zero-shot and few-shot learning] push generalization further: the model\n188\thandles new tasks with no labeled examples at all (zero-shot) or only a handful\n189\t(few-shot). Large language models such as GPT-4 demonstrate this by solving\n190\tnovel tasks purely through zero-shot prompting #cite(\"openai2023gpt4\"), relying\n191\ton broad pretraining rather than task-specific supervision.\n192\t\n193\t#strong[Active learning] flips the usual labeling workflow. Instead of passively\n194\treceiving labeled data, the model itself selects the most informative samples to\n195\tbe labeled by an oracle, typically a human annotator #cite(\"settles2009survey\").\n196\tA common strategy is to pick samples where the model is least confident,\n197\tconcentrating labeling effort where it will reduce uncertainty the most.\n198\t\n199\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:99 '* Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (3/3)'\n200\t// Slide: Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (3/3)\n201\t#strong[Machine Learning Paradigms: Examples (3/3)]\n202\t\n203\t#strong[Federated learning] trains models across decentralized devices without\n204\tsharing raw data #cite(\"mcmahan2017federated\"). Each participant (a phone, a\n205\thospital, a bank) keeps its data local and sends only model updates to a central\n206\tserver, which aggregates them into a single improved model. This preserves\n207\tprivacy by design: the raw records never leave their origin. A typical\n208\tapplication is fraud detection or credit scoring across multiple banks, where\n209\tpooling the underlying transaction data would violate regulatory constraints,\n210\tyet each institution benefits from patterns visible only in the combined\n211\tpopulation.\n212\t\n213\t#strong[Evolutionary learning] optimizes model structures or parameters through\n214\talgorithms inspired by natural selection and genetics. A population of candidate\n215\tsolutions is maintained; each generation, the fittest individuals are selected,\n216\trecombined, and mutated to produce offspring that (on average) perform better.\n217\tBecause the process relies on fitness evaluation rather than gradient\n218\tcomputation, it is #emph[gradient-free], making it applicable to discrete,\n219\tnon-differentiable, or highly multimodal search spaces where backpropagation\n220\tcannot reach. Genetic algorithms are the most familiar instance, but the family\n221\talso includes evolution strategies, genetic programming, and neuroevolution.\n222\t\n223\t#strong[Curriculum learning] structures the training process so that a model\n224\tencounters easier examples or tasks first, with difficulty increasing gradually\n225\tover time #cite(\"bengio2009curriculum\"). The intuition mirrors human education:\n226\tmastering arithmetic before calculus builds representations that transfer\n227\tupward. In practice, a curriculum can be defined by hand (sorting training\n228\tsamples by a known difficulty score) or learned automatically (letting the\n229\ttraining loop decide which examples to present next). Robotic control is a\n230\tnatural fit: a simulated robot can first learn to balance, then walk, then\n231\tnavigate obstacles, with each stage providing a foundation for the next.\n232\t\n233\t#strong[Multi-agent learning] places multiple agents in a shared environment\n234\twhere they learn simultaneously, often under game-theoretic dynamics such as\n235\tcompetition, cooperation, or a mix of both. Because each agent's optimal policy\n236\tdepends on what the others are doing, the learning problem is fundamentally\n237\tnon-stationary: the \"environment\" shifts as every participant adapts. DeepMind's\n238\tAlphaStar system #cite(\"vinyals2019alphastar\") illustrates the approach at\n239\tscale: a league of agents trained against one another in StarCraft II, producing\n240\tstrategies that reached Grandmaster-level play against human professionals. The\n241\tcompetitive pressure drove the discovery of diverse tactics that no single-agent\n242\ttraining regime would have uncovered.\n243\t\n244\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:122 '## The Three Core Paradigms'\n245\t// Slide: The Three Core Paradigms\n246\t== The Three Core Paradigms\n247\t\n248\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:124 '* Supervised Learning'\n249\t// Slide: Supervised Learning\n250\t#strong[Supervised Learning]\n251\t\n252\t#strong[Supervised learning] learns a function $f: X arrow.r Y$ that maps inputs\n253\tto correct outputs #cite(\"mitchell1997machinelearning\"). The training set\n254\tconsists of example pairs $(bold(x), y)$, where each input $bold(x)$ is paired\n255\twith the correct output $y$. Because every training example carries a label\n256\t$y_i$, supervised learning requires labeled data, and performance is measured by\n257\tthe error the learned function makes on a separate test set that was held out\n258\tduring training.\n259\t\n260\tTwo main task types fall under this umbrella. #emph[Classification] produces a\n261\tdiscrete label: an email filter that outputs \"Spam\" or \"Not Spam,\" a digit\n262\trecognizer that returns one of the digits 0 through 9, or a sentiment analyzer\n263\tthat labels text as positive, negative, or neutral. #emph[Regression], by\n264\tcontrast, produces a continuous value: predicting house prices from features\n265\tlike size and location, forecasting oil demand, or estimating future stock\n266\tprices. The choice between classification and regression is determined by the\n267\tnature of the output variable, not by the algorithm itself; many model families\n268\t(linear models, decision trees, neural networks) can be adapted to either\n269\tsetting.\n270\t\n271\tCommon supervised learning algorithms include linear regression, decision trees,\n272\tand neural networks, among many others. Each makes different assumptions about\n273\tthe shape of $f$ and trades off interpretability against expressive power, a\n274\ttheme that recurs throughout the course.\n275\t\n276\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:145 '* Unsupervised Learning'\n277\t// Slide: Unsupervised Learning\n278\t#strong[Unsupervised Learning]\n279\t\n280\t#strong[Unsupervised learning] learns from data without labeled outputs. Rather\n281\tthan receiving explicit feedback or correct answers, the algorithm's goal is to\n282\tdiscover patterns, groupings, or structure hidden within the data itself.\n283\tBecause there is no ground-truth label to compare against, evaluation tends to\n284\tbe more qualitative than in supervised settings: a practitioner judges whether\n285\tthe discovered structure is meaningful, useful, or interpretable for the task at\n286\thand.\n287\t\n288\tSeveral families of techniques fall under this umbrella:\n289\t\n290\t- #emph[Clustering] groups similar examples together. A retailer might segment\n291\t  its customers into behaviorally distinct groups to tailor marketing campaigns,\n292\t  or a news aggregator might group articles by topic without anyone having\n293\t  pre-assigned topic labels.\n294\t- #emph[Dimensionality reduction] compresses data from many variables down to\n295\t  fewer ones while preserving as much structure as possible. A common\n296\t  application is visualizing high-dimensional datasets in two dimensions using\n297\t  methods such as PCA, making it easier to spot clusters or outliers by eye.\n298\t- #emph[Density estimation] fits a probability distribution to the observed\n299\t  data. One practical use is anomaly detection: after learning what \"normal\"\n300\t  server-log traffic looks like, any observation that falls in a low-density\n301\t  region of the estimated distribution can be flagged as suspicious.\n302\t- #emph[Association rule learning] uncovers interesting relationships among\n303\t  variables. The classic example is market-basket analysis, where the algorithm\n304\t  discovers rules like \"customers who buy product X also tend to buy product Y,\"\n305\t  enabling cross-selling and store-layout decisions.\n306\t\n307\tRepresentative algorithms span all of these families. K-means #cite(\n308\t  \"macqueen1967kmeans\",\n309\t) is perhaps the most widely known clustering method, partitioning data into $k$\n310\tgroups by iteratively assigning points to their nearest centroid. PCA (Principal\n311\tComponent Analysis) is the workhorse of linear dimensionality reduction,\n312\tprojecting data onto the directions of greatest variance. Autoencoders, a\n313\tneural-network approach, learn a compressed latent representation by training\n314\tthe network to reconstruct its own input through a narrow bottleneck layer, and\n315\tthey can serve both dimensionality reduction and density estimation purposes\n316\tdepending on the architecture.\n317\t\n318\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:167 '* Reinforcement Learning'\n319\t// Slide: Reinforcement Learning\n320\t#strong[Reinforcement Learning]\n321\t\n322\t#strong[Reinforcement learning] (RL) is a paradigm in which an agent learns by\n323\tinteracting with an environment to maximize cumulative reward #cite(\n324\t  \"suttonbarto2018rlbook\",\n325\t). Rather than learning from a fixed dataset of labeled examples, the agent\n326\tdiscovers which actions yield the best outcomes through trial and error.\n327\tFormally, the goal is to learn a policy $pi(s) arrow.r a$ that maximizes\n328\texpected reward over time. A central tension in RL is the tradeoff between\n329\t#emph[exploration], trying new actions to discover potentially better\n330\tstrategies, and #emph[exploitation], relying on actions already known to produce\n331\tgood results. Balancing these two drives is essential: too much exploration\n332\twastes time on poor choices, while too much exploitation risks missing superior\n333\tstrategies entirely.\n334\t\n335\tOne of the practical difficulties of RL is that reward signals can be sparse,\n336\tdelayed, or hard to specify outside tightly controlled settings such as games\n337\tand simulators. When an agent receives a reward only at the end of a long\n338\tsequence of decisions, figuring out which earlier actions actually contributed\n339\tto success (the #emph[credit assignment] problem) becomes considerably harder.\n340\tRL tasks also often involve physical simulation or real-world interaction, which\n341\tadds cost and risk to every exploratory step the agent takes.\n342\t\n343\tThe core components of any RL system are straightforward. The #emph[agent] is\n344\tthe learner and decision maker. The #emph[environment] is everything the agent\n345\tinteracts with, including any dynamics, physics, or rules that govern how the\n346\tworld responds to the agent's choices. At each time step the environment is in\n347\tsome #emph[state] $s$, the agent selects an #emph[action] $a$, and the\n348\tenvironment returns a #emph[reward] $r$ along with the next state.\n349\t@fig:reinforcementlearning illustrates this interaction loop: the agent observes\n350\tthe current state, chooses an action, and receives both a reward and a new state\n351\tfrom the environment, then repeats.\n352\t\n353\t// rendered_images:begin\n354\t// ```graphviz\n355\t// digraph BayesianFlow {\n356\t//     splines=true;\n357\t//     nodesep=1.0;\n358\t//     ranksep=0.75;\n359\t// \n360\t//     node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n361\t// \n362\t//     // Node styles\n363\t//     Agent      [label=\"Agent\", shape=box, fillcolor=\"#F4A6A6\"];\n364\t//     Env        [label=\"Environment\", shape=box, fillcolor=\"#B2E2B2\"];\n365\t// \n366\t//     // Force ranks\n367\t//     //{ rank=same; Agent; Env; }\n368\t// \n369\t//     // Edges\n370\t//     Agent -> Env [label=\"  Action\", fontcolor=black, labeldistance=2.0];\n371\t//     Env -> Agent [label=\"  State\", fontcolor=black, labeldistance=2.0];\n372\t//     Env -> Agent [label=\"  Reward\", fontcolor=black, labeldistance=2.0];\n373\t// }\n374\t// ```\n375\t// label=fig:reinforcementlearning caption=Diagram relating Agent, Environment,\n376\t// rendered_images:end\n377\t// render_images:begin\n378\t#figure(\n379\t  image(\n380\t    \"Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.typ.figs/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.2.png\",\n381\t    width: 70%,\n382\t  ),\n383\t  kind: \"figure\",\n384\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n385\t  placement: auto,\n386\t) <fig:reinforcementlearning caption=Diagram relating Agent, Environment,>\n387\t// render_images:end\n388\tAction and State\n389\t\n390\tAmong the best-known RL algorithms are #emph[Q-learning], which maintains a\n391\ttable or function approximator estimating the expected future reward for each\n392\tstate-action pair, and #emph[policy gradient methods], which directly optimize\n393\tthe policy by adjusting its parameters in the direction that increases expected\n394\treward. These two families represent the main algorithmic divide in RL:\n395\tvalue-based methods that learn what states and actions are worth, versus\n396\tpolicy-based methods that learn the mapping from states to actions directly.\n397\t\n398\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:219 '* Reinforcement Learning: Examples'\n399\t// Slide: Reinforcement Learning: Examples\n400\t#strong[Reinforcement Learning: Examples]\n401\t\n402\tReinforcement learning finds natural application in any domain where an agent\n403\tmust make a sequence of decisions and can learn from the outcomes of those\n404\tdecisions over time.\n405\t\n406\t#strong[Game playing] stands as one of the most visible success stories: agents\n407\tlearn strategies through trial and error, with AlphaGo's mastery of Go serving\n408\tas a landmark demonstration that RL can surpass human expertise even in games\n409\twith enormous state spaces #cite(\"silver2016alphago\"). #strong[Robotics] relies\n410\ton RL to learn control policies for movement and manipulation, allowing robots\n411\tto acquire motor skills that would be extremely difficult to program by hand.\n412\t#strong[Autonomous driving] applies similar principles to learn safe and\n413\tefficient driving behaviors, where the agent must continuously balance speed,\n414\tsafety, and traffic rules in a dynamic environment.\n415\t\n416\tBeyond physical control, RL excels at #strong[resource management] problems that\n417\trequire optimizing the allocation of limited resources over time. Data center\n418\tcooling systems, for instance, can learn energy-efficient temperature policies,\n419\tand CPU job schedulers can learn to balance throughput against latency without\n420\texplicit hand-tuned heuristics. #strong[Personalized recommendations] represent\n421\tanother natural fit: a recommendation system adapts its suggestions based on\n422\tongoing user interaction, treating each click or skip as a reward signal that\n423\tshapes future rankings (a newsfeed adjusting its story selection in response to\n424\treading patterns is a canonical example). Finally, #strong[healthcare]\n425\tapplications use RL to optimize treatment plans over time, sequencing\n426\tmedications or therapies in a way that accounts for a patient's evolving\n427\tcondition rather than following a single static protocol.\n428\t\n429\tThe common thread across all these domains is that decisions are sequential,\n430\tfeedback is delayed or partial, and the environment shifts in response to the\n431\tagent's own actions: precisely the setting where reinforcement learning offers\n432\tthe most leverage over traditional supervised approaches.\n433\t\n434\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:232 '## Machine Learning in Practice'\n435\t// Slide: Machine Learning in Practice\n436\t== Machine Learning in Practice\n437\t\n438\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:234 '* Machine Learning Flow (1/2)'\n439\t// Slide: Machine Learning Flow (1/2)\n440\t#strong[Machine Learning Flow (1/2)]\n441\t\n442\tEvery machine learning project follows a common pipeline whose stages build on\n443\tone another. The process begins with a #strong[question]: a concrete problem\n444\tstatement such as \"how can we predict house prices?\" That question determines\n445\twhat #emph[input data] you need; for the house-price example, this would be\n446\thistorical records of house sales including sale prices and property attributes.\n447\tFrom the raw data you extract #emph[features], the individual measurable\n448\tproperties the model will learn from: number of bedrooms, neighborhood location,\n449\tsquare footage, and so on. Next you choose a #emph[model], the mathematical\n450\tstructure that will map features to predictions (a linear regression, a decision\n451\ttree, or something more complex). Every model comes with #emph[parameters] that\n452\tcontrol how it learns or how complex it becomes: the learning rate that governs\n453\tgradient-descent step sizes, or the number of trees in a random forest. Finally,\n454\t#emph[evaluation] closes the loop: you measure the trained model's quality with\n455\tmetrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall, and those results feed back\n456\tinto refining earlier stages (collecting better data, engineering new features,\n457\tor tuning parameters).\n458\t\n459\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:244 '* Machine Learning Flow (2/2)'\n460\t// Slide: Machine Learning Flow (2/2)\n461\t#strong[Machine Learning Flow (2/2)]\n462\t\n463\t// rendered_images:begin\n464\t// ```graphviz\n465\t// digraph BayesianFlow {\n466\t//     rankdir=LR;\n467\t//     splines=true;\n468\t//     nodesep=1.0;\n469\t//     ranksep=0.75;\n470\t//     node [shape=box, style=\"rounded,filled\", fontname=\"Helvetica\", fontsize=12, penwidth=1.4];\n471\t//     // Node styles\n472\t//     \"Question\" [fillcolor=\"#F4A6A6\"];\n473\t//     \"Input data\" [fillcolor=\"#FFD1A6\"];\n474\t//     \"Features\" [fillcolor=\"#B2E2B2\"];\n475\t//     \"Model\" [fillcolor=\"#A0D6D1\"];\n476\t//     \"Parameters\" [fillcolor=\"#A6E7F4\"];\n477\t//     \"Evaluation\" [fillcolor=\"#A6C8F4\"];\n478\t//     // Force ranks\n479\t//     // Edges\n480\t//     \"Question\" -> \"Input data\";\n481\t//     \"Input data\" -> \"Features\";\n482\t//     \"Features\" -> \"Model\";\n483\t//     \"Model\" -> \"Parameters\";\n484\t//     \"Parameters\" -> \"Evaluation\";\n485\t// }\n486\t// ```\n487\t// label=fig:machinelearningflow22 caption=Diagram illustrating Machine Learning\n488\t// rendered_images:end\n489\t// render_images:begin\n490\t#figure(\n491\t  image(\n492\t    \"Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.typ.figs/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.3.png\",\n493\t    width: 70%,\n494\t  ),\n495\t  kind: \"figure\",\n496\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n497\t  placement: auto,\n498\t) <fig:machinelearningflow22 caption=Diagram illustrating Machine Learning>\n499\t// render_images:end\n500\tFlow (2/2)\n501\t\n502\tNot all phases in the machine learning workflow carry equal weight. A useful\n503\trule of thumb ranks them as: question, then data, then features, then model. The\n504\tclarity of the #emph[question] you ask has the single largest impact on whether\n505\ta project succeeds or fails; a vague or poorly scoped question can doom even the\n506\tmost sophisticated pipeline. Next comes the quality and relevance of the\n507\t#emph[data]: no algorithm can extract signal that the data never contained.\n508\tProper #emph[feature] selection simplifies the downstream model and often\n509\timproves accuracy more than swapping one learner for another. The #emph[model]\n510\titself, contrary to popular belief, is frequently the least decisive factor. As\n511\t@fig:machinelearningflow22 illustrates, the earlier stages of the flow constrain\n512\teverything that follows, so investing effort upstream pays disproportionate\n513\tdividends compared to tuning the learning algorithm at the end.\n514\t\n515\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:277 '* Framing the Question'\n516\t// Slide: Framing the Question\n517\t#strong[Framing the Question]\n518\t\n519\tFormulating the question is the most important part of any machine learning\n520\tproblem. A misunderstanding at this stage cascades into everything that follows:\n521\tsolving the wrong problem, collecting the wrong data, and producing results that\n522\tserve no one. As Einstein reportedly put it, \"If I were given one hour to save\n523\tthe planet, I would spend 59 minutes defining the problem and one minute\n524\tresolving it.\" Whether or not the attribution is genuine, the principle holds:\n525\tprecision in problem definition determines whether the rest of the work has any\n526\tvalue.\n527\t\n528\tMaking the question concrete and precise means aligning it with the actual\n529\tbusiness or research objective, then defining the problem in terms specific\n530\tenough to guide data collection and model selection. Consider the difference\n531\tbetween a vague question and a well-formed one:\n532\t\n533\t- #emph[Bad]: \"How can we improve sales?\"\n534\t- #emph[Good]: \"What factors most significantly impact sales of product X in\n535\t  region Y during season Z?\"\n536\t\n537\tThe first version gives no guidance on what data to gather, what outcome\n538\tvariable to model, or what \"improve\" even means. The second version pins down\n539\tthe product, the geographic scope, and the temporal window, which together\n540\tdetermine the dataset, the target variable, and the evaluation criteria. A\n541\twell-posed question is one where you can immediately see what a correct answer\n542\twould look like and how you would know if you had found it.\n543\t\n544\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:296 '* Input Data: Fit, Quality, and Scale'\n545\t// Slide: Input Data: Fit, Quality, and Scale\n546\t#strong[Input Data: Fit, Quality, and Scale]\n547\t\n548\tThe data used to build a predictive model must be specific to the prediction\n549\tgoal. If the task is to predict movie ratings, for instance, the training\n550\texamples should be known ratings drawn from the same population whose unseen\n551\tratings the model will eventually estimate. More precisely, the training set\n552\tshould approximate the test set, which in turn should approximate the data the\n553\tmodel will encounter in production. Any mismatch between these distributions\n554\tundermines the validity of the predictions.\n555\t\n556\tThe relationship between the available data and the ultimate prediction goal is\n557\tnot always direct. A business may care about future prices, yet the most\n558\teffective modeling strategy might be to predict supply and demand separately and\n559\tderive prices from those forecasts. Recognizing these indirect links, and\n560\tchoosing the right quantity to model, is itself a design decision that shapes\n561\tthe entire pipeline.\n562\t\n563\tData quality matters as much as data relevance. Poor-quality inputs, whether\n564\tnoisy, biased, or incomplete, propagate through every downstream step and\n565\tproduce unreliable outputs: #emph[\"garbage in, garbage out.\"] Equally important\n566\tis the discipline to recognize when the data at hand is simply insufficient to\n567\tanswer the question being asked. As John Tukey cautioned, #emph[\"desire for an\n568\t  answer does not ensure that a reasonable answer can be extracted from the\n569\t  given body of data.\"] Pressing forward with an inadequate dataset does not\n570\tyield a weaker answer; it yields a misleading one.\n571\t\n572\tA recurring empirical finding is that #strong[more data often matters more than\n573\t  a better model]. The gap between a well-tuned generic algorithm and the best\n574\thand-crafted specialist model is frequently small compared to the gain from\n575\tsimply adding more, or higher-quality, training examples. The sentiment is\n576\tcaptured by the observation that #emph[\"it's not who has the best algorithm that\n577\t  wins; it's who has the most data\"] #cite(\"banko2001data\"). A famous (and only\n578\thalf-joking) remark from an IBM speech-recognition researcher makes the same\n579\tpoint from the opposite direction: #emph[\"every time I fire a linguist, the\n580\t  performance of the speech recognizer goes up.\"] The lesson is not that\n581\tmodeling skill is irrelevant, but that in many practical settings, investing in\n582\tdata collection and curation yields higher returns than investing in algorithmic\n583\tsophistication alone.\n584\t\n585\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:320 '* What Makes a Good Feature'\n586\t// Slide: What Makes a Good Feature\n587\t#strong[What Makes a Good Feature]\n588\t\n589\t#strong[Features] are higher-level, more compact representations of raw inputs\n590\tthat capture the information most relevant to a learning task. Rather than\n591\tfeeding a model every pixel of a scanned digit image, for instance, you might\n592\textract just two numbers: the overall intensity and the vertical symmetry of the\n593\timage. Those two quantities compress thousands of pixel values into a pair of\n594\tinformative signals that a simple classifier can work with directly.\n595\t\n596\tGood features share three characteristics. First, they #emph[retain the\n597\t  information that matters] for distinguishing between classes or predicting a\n598\ttarget. Second, they #emph[compress the data], replacing a high-dimensional\n599\tinput with a much smaller vector and thereby reducing the computational and\n600\tstatistical burden on the learner. Third, they are #emph[often designed with\n601\t  expert knowledge]: a radiologist knows which texture statistics matter in a\n602\tchest X-ray, and a linguist knows which syntactic patterns signal sentiment in\n603\ttext.\n604\t\n605\tBuilding features by hand or by automated search is, however, a process prone to\n606\tseveral common mistakes:\n607\t\n608\t1. #emph[Automating feature selection without guarding against overfitting.] A\n609\t  search over a large feature space can find combinations that fit the training\n610\t  set perfectly yet capture nothing stable about the underlying phenomenon. The\n611\t  resulting model becomes a black box whose predictions are accurate on\n612\t  historical data but can stop working at any time. Google Flu Trends is a\n613\t  cautionary example: the system selected query terms that correlated with flu\n614\t  rates during one period, but the link between those features and the model's\n615\t  predictions was never made transparent, and performance degraded sharply when\n616\t  search behavior shifted.\n617\t\n618\t2. #emph[Ignoring data-specific quirks.] Every dataset has idiosyncrasies:\n619\t  measurement artifacts, coding conventions, or outliers that look like signal\n620\t  but are really noise. Mislabeling an outlier as a legitimate extreme, for\n621\t  example, can bias a feature's scale and skew everything downstream.\n622\t\n623\t3. #emph[Unnecessarily discarding information.] Aggressive feature selection or\n624\t  overly coarse binning can throw away structure that a model could have\n625\t  exploited. Compression is valuable, but it should be guided by relevance to\n626\t  the task, not by convenience. Whenever there is doubt about whether a piece of\n627\t  information matters, it is safer to keep it and let the learning algorithm\n628\t  decide than to discard it prematurely.\n629\t\n630\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:338 '* What Makes a Good Model'\n631\t// Slide: What Makes a Good Model\n632\t#strong[What Makes a Good Model]\n633\t\n634\tA good predictive model balances several desirable properties that often pull\n635\tagainst one another, as @fig:whatmakesagoodmodel illustrates. Understanding\n636\tthese tradeoffs is essential for choosing the right model for a given\n637\tapplication.\n638\t\n639\t// rendered_images:begin\n640\t// ```graphviz\n641\t// digraph ModelTradeoffs {\n642\t//     bgcolor=\"transparent\";\n643\t//     pad=\"0.15\";\n644\t//     splines=spline;\n645\t//     nodesep=0.5;\n646\t//     ranksep=0.6;\n647\t//     rankdir=TB;\n648\t// \n649\t//     node [shape=box,\n650\t//           style=\"rounded,filled\",\n651\t//           penwidth=1.8,\n652\t//           fontname=\"Helvetica\",\n653\t//           fontsize=11,\n654\t//           margin=\"0.18,0.10\",\n655\t//           height=0.45];\n656\t// \n657\t//     edge [style=dashed,\n658\t//           color=\"#B23A48\",\n659\t//           penwidth=1.3,\n660\t//           arrowhead=none,\n661\t//           fontname=\"Helvetica\",\n662\t//           fontsize=9,\n663\t//           fontcolor=\"#6B1F1F\"];\n664\t// \n665\t//     Accurate      [label=\"Accurate\", fillcolor=\"#9CC4F2\", color=\"#3C6FB0\", fontcolor=\"#1F4E79\", penwidth=2.4];\n666\t//     Interpretable [label=\"Interpretable\", fillcolor=\"#A9DDB0\", color=\"#4F9A5C\", fontcolor=\"#1F4E2E\"];\n667\t//     Simple        [label=\"Simple\", fillcolor=\"#A9DDB0\", color=\"#4F9A5C\", fontcolor=\"#1F4E2E\"];\n668\t//     Fast          [label=\"Fast\", fillcolor=\"#A9DDB0\", color=\"#4F9A5C\", fontcolor=\"#1F4E2E\"];\n669\t//     Scalable      [label=\"Scalable\", fillcolor=\"#A9DDB0\", color=\"#4F9A5C\", fontcolor=\"#1F4E2E\"];\n670\t// \n671\t//     { rank=same; Interpretable; Simple; Fast; Scalable; }\n672\t// \n673\t//     Accurate -> Interpretable [label=\"  Trade-off  \"];\n674\t//     Accurate -> Simple [label=\"  Overfitting risk  \"];\n675\t//     Accurate -> Fast [label=\"  Compute cost  \"];\n676\t//     Accurate -> Scalable [label=\"  Resources  \"];\n677\t// }\n678\t// ```\n679\t// label=fig:whatmakesagoodmodel caption=Diagram relating Accurate, Interpretable,\n680\t// rendered_images:end\n681\t// render_images:begin\n682\t#figure(\n683\t  image(\n684\t    \"Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.typ.figs/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.4.png\",\n685\t    width: 70%,\n686\t  ),\n687\t  kind: \"figure\",\n688\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n689\t  placement: auto,\n690\t) <fig:whatmakesagoodmodel caption=Diagram relating Accurate, Interpretable,>\n691\t// render_images:end\n692\tSimple and Fast\n693\t\n694\t#strong[Simplicity] makes a model easier to implement, maintain, and debug.\n695\tSimpler models also carry a lower risk of overfitting, since they have fewer\n696\tparameters that can latch onto noise in the training data rather than genuine\n697\tpatterns.\n698\t\n699\t#strong[Accuracy] is typically what practitioners optimize first, yet pushing\n700\taccuracy higher often comes at the expense of every other property. A highly\n701\taccurate ensemble of dozens of models may be too slow to deploy, too complex to\n702\texplain, and too brittle to maintain.\n703\t\n704\t#strong[Interpretability] lets users understand and trust the decisions a model\n705\tproduces. Decision trees, for instance, excel here because they output an\n706\texplicit chain of reasoning: each prediction can be traced back through a\n707\tsequence of human-readable conditions. In domains such as healthcare or criminal\n708\tjustice, interpretability is not optional; stakeholders need to know #emph[why]\n709\ta model reached a particular conclusion.\n710\t\n711\t#strong[Speed] matters both at training time and at inference time. Real-time\n712\tapplications such as fraud detection or autonomous driving require predictions\n713\twithin milliseconds, ruling out models whose inference cost scales poorly with\n714\tinput size.\n715\t\n716\t#strong[Scalability] refers to how well a model handles growing datasets and\n717\tuser bases. A celebrated cautionary tale comes from the Netflix Prize: the\n718\twinning algorithm achieved the best accuracy on the competition's benchmark, yet\n719\tNetflix never deployed it in production because it was not scalable enough to\n720\tserve its millions of users at acceptable latency. Scalability thus acts as a\n721\thard gate; a model that cannot scale is a model that cannot ship, regardless of\n722\thow accurate it is on a static leaderboard.\n723\t\n724\tIn practice, model selection is an exercise in navigating these tensions.\n725\tImproving one property almost always degrades another, so the \"best\" model is\n726\talways relative to the constraints of the problem at hand.\n727\t\n728\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:407 '## Pipeline Organization'\n729\t// Slide: Pipeline Organization\n730\t== Pipeline Organization\n731\t\n732\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:409 '* How Are Machine Learning Systems Organized?'\n733\t// Slide: How Are Machine Learning Systems Organized?\n734\t#strong[How Are Machine Learning Systems Organized?]\n735\t\n736\tMachine learning systems are organized as a #strong[pipeline]: a sequence of\n737\tstages where the problem is broken down into sub-problems, each sub-problem is\n738\tsolved in turn, and the individual solutions are combined to address the\n739\toriginal problem.\n740\t\n741\tA critical property of pipelines is that overall system performance $p_\"system\"$\n742\tis not simply a weighted sum of the per-stage performances $p_i$. Instead,\n743\t#emph[stage errors compound]: a mistake early in the pipeline propagates through\n744\tevery subsequent stage, degrading the final output far more than the magnitude\n745\tof the original error might suggest. This compounding effect means that\n746\timproving a late stage may yield little benefit if an earlier stage is already\n747\tcorrupting its input.\n748\t\n749\t#strong[Ceiling analysis] provides a principled way to measure each stage's\n750\tmarginal contribution to system performance. The idea is to replace one stage at\n751\ta time with a perfect \"oracle\" and observe how much the end-to-end metric\n752\timproves. Formally, the relationship is approximated as\n753\t\n754\t$ Delta p_\"system\" approx alpha_i dot.op Delta p_i $\n755\t\n756\twhere $Delta p_i$ is the improvement in the performance of stage $i$ alone (for\n757\tinstance, by substituting an oracle for that stage) and $alpha_i$ is the\n758\tresulting improvement in overall system performance. Stages with large $alpha_i$\n759\tare the bottlenecks worth investing effort in, while stages whose oracle\n760\treplacement barely moves the system metric can be deprioritized.\n761\t\n762\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:431 '* Example of Photo OCR System'\n763\t// Slide: Example of Photo OCR System\n764\t#strong[Example of Photo OCR System]\n765\t\n766\tThe goal of #strong[optical character recognition] (OCR) is to build systems\n767\tthat can read text appearing in a photograph or scanned document. This task is\n768\tmore challenging than it might first seem: text in natural images varies in\n769\tfont, size, orientation, lighting, and background clutter, so a robust OCR\n770\tpipeline must handle each of these sources of variability systematically.\n771\t\n772\tA typical ML pipeline for OCR breaks the problem into four sequential stages.\n773\tFirst, #emph[text detection] locates regions of the image that contain text.\n774\tSecond, #emph[character segmentation] splits each detected text region into\n775\tindividual letter boxes (for instance, the word \"hello\" becomes five separate\n776\tbounding boxes: `h`, `e`, `l`, `l`, `o`). Third, #emph[character classification]\n777\tidentifies each segmented box as a specific character. Finally, #emph[spelling\n778\t  correction] uses linguistic context to fix recognition errors: if the\n779\tclassifier output `hell0` (with a zero instead of the letter \"o\"), the\n780\tcorrection step maps it to the intended word \"hello.\" Each stage feeds its\n781\toutput to the next, so errors can compound; building an accurate classifier at\n782\tevery stage is therefore critical.\n783\t\n784\t// rendered_images:begin\n785\t// ```graphviz\n786\t// digraph OCRPipeline {\n787\t//     bgcolor=\"transparent\";\n788\t//     pad=\"0.15\";\n789\t// label=fig:exampleofphotoocrsystem caption=Diagram relating Input image, Text\n825\t// rendered_images:end\n826\t// render_images:begin\n827\t#figure(\n828\t  image(\n829\t    \"Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.typ.figs/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.5.png\",\n830\t    width: 70%,\n831\t  ),\n832\t  kind: \"figure\",\n833\t  supplement: [Fig.],\n834\t  placement: auto,\n835\t) <fig:exampleofphotoocrsystem caption=Diagram relating Input image, Text>\n836\t// render_images:end\n837\tdetection, Character segmentation and Character classification\n838\t\n839\t@fig:exampleofphotoocrsystem illustrates how these four stages connect, showing\n840\tthe flow from a raw input image through detection, segmentation, and\n841\tclassification to a final text string.\n842\t\n843\tBecause the location and size of text in a natural image are unknown in advance,\n844\ta #strong[sliding window approach] is used to search for text systematically.\n845\tFor the text detection stage, the idea is to train a binary classifier that\n846\tdistinguishes windows containing letters from windows containing only\n847\tbackground. This is a simpler learning problem than recognizing which letter a\n848\twindow contains; the classifier only needs to say \"text\" or \"not text.\" At\n849\tinference time, the trained classifier is swept across the image in both the\n850\thorizontal and vertical directions, evaluated at multiple window scales to\n851\thandle text of different sizes. Evaluating the classifier on a single window is\n852\tcomputationally cheap, so this exhaustive scan remains practical even for large\n853\timages.\n854\t\n855\tThe classifier's output probabilities are assembled into a #emph[text likelihood\n856\t  map], essentially a heatmap where bright regions indicate a high probability\n857\tof text. Connected high-probability regions are then enclosed in bounding boxes.\n858\tBoxes whose aspect ratio is inconsistent with real text (for example, a box that\n859\tis taller than it is wide, since valid text regions are almost always wider than\n860\tthey are tall) are discarded as false positives. The same sliding window\n861\tstrategy is then reused for the character segmentation stage: a second\n862\tclassifier, trained to distinguish boundaries between characters from the\n863\tinterior of a character, is swept across each detected text region to find the\n864\tsplits between individual letters.\n865\t\n866\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:494 '* Getting More Data'\n867\t// Slide: Getting More Data\n868\t#strong[Getting More Data]\n869\t\n870\tThe ideal recipe for machine learning is straightforward: combine a\n871\t#emph[low-bias algorithm] with a #emph[massive amount of data]. A low-bias model\n872\thas enough capacity to capture complex patterns, and abundant data prevents it\n873\tfrom overfitting to noise. The challenge lies in making this recipe practical.\n874\t\n875\tHow do we know we are using the data effectively? One concrete tool is\n876\t#strong[learning curves], which plot training and validation performance as a\n877\tfunction of dataset size. If the validation curve is still climbing steeply when\n878\tyou run out of data, you have room to benefit from more. If both curves have\n879\tplateaued and converged, adding data alone will not help, and you should instead\n880\tlook at model capacity or feature engineering.\n881\t\n882\tHow do we actually get a large amount of data? A useful habit is to ask: \"how\n883\tmuch work would it take to get 10x more data than we currently have?\" The answer\n884\tis often less daunting than expected, and two broad strategies cover most\n885\tsituations:\n886\t\n887\t- #emph[Artificial data]: synthesize or augment an existing dataset. In computer\n888\t  vision this might mean applying rotations, crops, color jitter, or generative\n889\t  models to produce realistic variants. In NLP, paraphrasing or back-translation\n890\t  can multiply a corpus. The key constraint is that the synthetic examples must\n891\t  stay close to the true data distribution; otherwise the extra volume hurts\n892\t  more than it helps.\n893\t- #emph[Collect and label by hand]: crowdsourcing platforms such as Amazon\n894\t  Mechanical Turk let you scale human annotation relatively cheaply, though\n895\t  quality control (redundant labeling, gold-standard checks) is essential. More\n896\t  recently, large language models have been used to generate or annotate data,\n897\t  but this carries real risk: the model's own biases and errors propagate into\n898\t  your training set, so any LLM-generated labels should be treated as noisy and\n899\t  validated against human judgment.\n900\t\n901\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:511 '* Getting Mode Data: OCR Pipeline'\n902\t// Slide: Getting Mode Data: OCR Pipeline\n903\t#strong[Getting Mode Data: OCR Pipeline]\n904\t\n905\tHow can we increase the size of a training set for a problem like optical\n906\tcharacter recognition (OCR)? Several practical strategies exist, ranging from\n907\tfully synthetic generation to human-powered collection.\n908\t\n909\t1. #emph[Synthesize a data set from scratch]: use font libraries to render\n910\t  characters in many typefaces, paste them against random backgrounds, and apply\n911\t  transformations such as scaling, rotation, distortion, and additive noise.\n912\t  This can produce virtually unlimited labeled examples at negligible marginal\n913\t  cost.\n914\t2. #emph[Amplify an existing data set]: take real examples already in hand and\n915\t  generate new ones by warping, distorting, or otherwise perturbing them. The\n916\t  result is a larger and more varied training set without collecting any new raw\n917\t  data.\n918\t3. #emph[Distill other models]: use a larger, already-trained model to label a\n919\t  pool of unlabeled data, then train a smaller model on those soft or hard\n920\t  labels.\n921\t4. #emph[Buy or create datasets]: acquire labeled data from commercial providers\n922\t  or invest in building a bespoke collection pipeline.\n923\t5. #emph[Crowdsourcing and gamification]: distribute labeling tasks to a large\n924\t  pool of human workers, sometimes embedding the work inside a game to improve\n925\t  engagement and throughput.\n926\t\n927\tFor strategies 1 and 2, the choice of transformations and noise must be guided\n928\tby the application domain. Gaussian noise, for instance, is a common default,\n929\tbut it may not reflect the actual degradation a system encounters in practice.\n930\tAn OCR system reading scanned documents faces ink bleed, uneven lighting, and\n931\tpaper texture, none of which look like isotropic Gaussian perturbations.\n932\tApplying domain-inappropriate augmentations can introduce a mismatch between\n933\ttraining and deployment distributions, ultimately hurting rather than helping\n934\tgeneralization.\n935\t\n936\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:528 '* Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline'\n937\t// Slide: Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline\n938\t#strong[Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline]\n939\t\n940\tThe most valuable resource in any machine learning project is time. Researchers'\n941\ttime is extremely expensive, and spending months optimizing one component of a\n942\tpipeline only to discover that the optimization barely moves the needle on\n943\toverall performance is a costly mistake. The central question, then, is: which\n944\tpart of the pipeline deserves the investment of time and resources?\n945\t\n946\t#strong[Ceiling analysis] provides a principled answer by quantifying how much\n947\teach pipeline component limits end-to-end performance. The procedure begins by\n948\tchoosing a single scalar metric for the entire system, since juggling too many\n949\tmetrics at once obscures the signal (for an OCR system, for instance, overall\n950\tcharacter-level accuracy works well). Then, working through the pipeline in\n951\torder, each component is temporarily replaced by an \"oracle\" that always\n952\tproduces the correct output while every other component is left untouched. After\n953\teach such replacement the end-to-end metric is recomputed. The component whose\n954\toracle produces the largest jump in that metric is the highest-value target for\n955\tfurther work: it is the bottleneck whose errors propagate most heavily through\n956\tthe rest of the system.\n957\t\n958\tThe key discipline ceiling analysis enforces is measurement over intuition. It\n959\tis tempting to optimize whichever stage feels most imperfect or most\n960\tintellectually interesting, but as Knuth warned, \"premature optimization is the\n961\troot of all evil\" #cite(\"knuth1974premature\"). Without ceiling analysis, teams\n962\troutinely pour effort into a stage that is already performing near its ceiling\n963\twhile ignoring the true bottleneck one or two steps away.\n964\t\n965\t// From: msml610/lectures_source/Lesson02.2-ML_Paradigms.smd:552 '* Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline: OCT Example'\n966\t// Slide: Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline: OCT Example\n967\t#strong[Ceiling Analysis for ML Pipeline: OCT Example]\n968\t\n969\tConsider a concrete example: an OCR pipeline whose baseline accuracy is 72%. A\n970\tceiling analysis reveals which component deserves attention first. As\n971\t@tab:ceilinganalysisformlpipelineoctexample shows, text detection is the\n972\thighest-value target: perfecting it alone accounts for most of the achievable\n973\tgain. The remaining components, while still imperfect, contribute far less\n974\tmarginal improvement, so engineering effort spent on them yields diminishing\n975\treturns until the text detection bottleneck is resolved.\n976\t\n977\t#figure(\n978\t  styled-table(\n979\t    headers: (\"Component made perfect\", \"Accuracy\", \"Gain\"),\n980\t    rows: (\n981\t      (\"(baseline system)\", \"72%\", \"--\"),\n982\t      (\"Text detection\", \"89%\", \"+17%\"),\n983\t      (\"+ Char. segmentation\", \"90%\", \"+1%\"),\n984\t      (\"+ Char. classification\", \"100%\", \"+10%\"),\n985\t
